prosecution_strengths: Officers in South Dakota are trained on standardized NHTSA field sobriety testing, and courts give significant weight to the HGN (horizontal gaze nystagmus) test as a scientific indicator.
Prosecutors may charge based solely on actual physical control (engine off, keys in pocket can suffice) — the state need not prove the vehicle was in motion.
defense_opportunities: Attack chemical test foundation: South Dakota requires a 20-minute observation period before breath testing under SD Admin Rules 64:37, and any contamination invalidates results.
Source code/maintenance records for the Intoxilyzer 8000 are discoverable in South Dakota and can reveal calibration issues.
Question whether the defendant was in 'actual physical control' if the vehicle was parked, off, and the defendant was not in the driver's seat.
Review the dashcam and bodycam footage against the officer's report — discrepancies in recorded driving patterns versus narrative reports often produce suppression motions.
common_defenses: Lack of reasonable suspicion for the initial stop (Fourth Amendment suppression).
Improper administration of field sobriety tests (medical conditions, footwear, surface, lighting).
Rising blood alcohol defense — BAC was below limit while driving and rose during the delay before testing.
Medical conditions mimicking intoxication (diabetes, GERD/acid reflux causing mouth alcohol, neurological conditions).
Chain of custody or calibration failures with the breath or blood testing instrument.

prosecution_strengths: First-offense DUI in South Dakota requires no proof of prior history, simplifying the prosecution's case.
Class 1 Misdemeanor classification allows prosecution in magistrate court with streamlined procedures.
Prosecutors can use the implied consent advisory and refusal as substantive evidence.
Courts routinely admit BAC evidence with minimal foundational challenges in first-offense cases.
defense_opportunities: Negotiation toward reckless driving (a 'wet reckless') is possible when chemical test results are weak.
Challenge the 20-minute observation rule for breath testing — common compliance failures.
Invoke administrative hearing rights within 30 days to contest license revocation separately from criminal case.
common_defenses: Breath test machine maintenance and calibration deficiencies.
Officer failure to follow NHTSA SFST protocol.
Necessity or duress (rare but recognized when fleeing immediate harm).

prosecution_strengths: South Dakota maintains a centralized DUI tracking system through the Department of Public Safety, making prior convictions easy to prove.
Mandatory minimum jail time applies to repeat offenders, eliminating probation-only outcomes.
Permanent ignition interlock requirements apply for third+ offenses.
Felony classification enables longer probation tails and broader collateral consequences.
defense_opportunities: Challenge the validity of prior convictions on Boykin grounds (proper plea colloquy, knowing waiver of rights).
Out-of-state prior convictions must be substantially similar to SD DUI law to count as predicates — analyze each carefully.
Negotiate down to a non-DUI alcohol offense if the chemical test is suppressible.
24/7 Sobriety Program participation can mitigate sentencing exposure even for repeat offenders.
Challenge the 10-year lookback calculation when prior convictions are near the threshold.
common_defenses: Constitutional invalidity of prior convictions used for enhancement.
Double jeopardy challenges to administrative + criminal penalties.
Same defenses as first-offense DUI applied to current charge.
Statute of limitations on stale priors.
Identity dispute when prior convictions belong to a different person with similar identifiers.

prosecution_strengths: Drug Recognition Experts (DREs) trained under the IACP protocol provide expert testimony on impairment.
Blood testing for drugs is admissible without breath test challenges.
Prescription medications can support DUI-drugs charges even when lawfully prescribed.
The state need not specify which drug caused impairment — any controlled substance suffices.
defense_opportunities: Challenge per se metabolite rule when defendant has medical marijuana or prescription history showing residual metabolites without impairment.
Attack DRE protocol — the 12-step DRE evaluation has known scientific weaknesses.
Question chain of custody for blood samples through the State Health Lab.
common_defenses: Lack of impairment despite presence of metabolites (especially marijuana).
Prescription medication defense with valid prescription and no warning labels violated.
Improper blood draw procedures (untrained phlebotomist, contaminated swab, wrong vial).

prosecution_strengths: Officer testimony alone often suffices for conviction; no scientific evidence required.
Often used as a fallback when DUI evidence is weak.
Court points and license suspension consequences create plea leverage.
Can be enhanced when combined with other moving violations on the same incident.
defense_opportunities: 'Wilful or wanton' is a high mens rea standard — mere negligence or carelessness is insufficient.
Challenge officer's vantage point and ability to observe alleged conduct.
Dashcam evidence frequently contradicts officer narratives about driving behavior.
Weather, road conditions, and emergency circumstances are mitigating factors.
common_defenses: Insufficient evidence of wilful or wanton conduct.
Mistake of fact regarding road conditions or traffic.

prosecution_strengths: Class 6 Felony classification (injury) and Class 5 Felony (death) make this a serious felony with significant exposure.
Vehicle damage and witness IDs frequently link defendants conclusively.
Knowledge of the accident can be inferred from circumstances (impact, debris, vehicle damage).
Surveillance cameras and license plate readers increasingly identify fleeing vehicles.
defense_opportunities: Attack the knowledge element — defendant must have known an accident occurred involving injury.
Identification defenses are common when only the vehicle is identified, not the driver.
Defendant returning to the scene within a reasonable time may negate intent.
Question whether the alleged 'accident' actually involved another vehicle or person.
Medical emergency exception when defendant left to seek aid.
common_defenses: Lack of knowledge that an accident occurred.
Necessity (medical emergency, threat to safety at scene).
Defendant did stop and provide information adequately.
No injury occurred (downgrade to misdemeanor leaving scene).

prosecution_strengths: Class 3 Felony with significant prison exposure (up to 15 years).
Medical examiner testimony establishing cause of death is typically uncontested.
Accident reconstruction experts provide compelling visual evidence.
BAC evidence carries enormous weight when paired with a fatality.
defense_opportunities: Causation is often the strongest defense — was the DUI actually the cause, or were other factors (other driver's actions, road conditions, mechanical failure) responsible?
Challenge BAC results aggressively given the stakes.
Independent accident reconstruction may show alternative causes.
Victim's contributory conduct (failure to wear seatbelt, sudden lane change) can mitigate or eliminate causation.
Negotiate to vehicular manslaughter (Class 4 Felony) when DUI evidence is borderline.
common_defenses: Insufficient proof of impairment at time of crash.
Constitutional challenges to blood draw without warrant.

prosecution_strengths: Lower mens rea standard than vehicular homicide makes conviction easier.
Class 4 Felony exposure still significant (up to 10 years).
Frequently charged as a fallback to vehicular homicide when DUI cannot be proven.
Eyewitness testimony about driving behavior is typically admissible without scientific foundation.
defense_opportunities: Criminal negligence requires gross deviation from reasonable care — argue the conduct was at most ordinary negligence (civil, not criminal).
Causation defenses are equally strong here as in vehicular homicide.
Accident reconstruction can show intervening or superseding causes.
Mechanical failure or unexpected medical event defenses.
Victim conduct contributing to the accident.
common_defenses: Conduct did not rise to criminal negligence.
Victim's own negligence as the proximate cause.

prosecution_strengths: DPS records easily prove the suspended status at the time of stop.
Class 2 Misdemeanor classification allows quick disposition.
Often charged alongside the original offense that caused the suspension, compounding penalties.
Subsequent offenses escalate to Class 1 Misdemeanor with mandatory jail time.
defense_opportunities: Challenge whether the defendant received proper notice of suspension under SD Department of Public Safety procedures.
Verify the underlying suspension was actually valid and not procedurally defective.
Mistake of fact regarding the date the suspension took effect or ended.
Hardship license eligibility may have been valid at time of stop.
Reinstatement may have technically occurred but not yet processed in DPS database.
common_defenses: Mistake of fact regarding license status.

prosecution_strengths: Class 5 Felony enhancement when fleeing creates substantial risk of injury or death.
Dashcam and bodycam evidence makes the elements easy to prove.
Officer testimony about lights, sirens, and visual contact is generally credible to juries.
Often paired with traffic offenses, DUI, or drug charges — significant charging leverage.
defense_opportunities: 'Willful' element requires defendant know an officer was attempting to stop the vehicle.
Lighting conditions, music volume, and distance can negate awareness of police signals.
Defendant pulling over at the next safe location is not necessarily fleeing.
Challenge the substantial risk enhancement — speed alone may not suffice.
GPS and event data recorder (EDR) evidence may contradict officer's claims about pursuit conditions.
common_defenses: Lack of willful intent (didn't know police were signaling).
Defendant was looking for a safe location to stop.
Officer signals were inadequate or non-conforming.

prosecution_strengths: Constructive possession doctrine allows charges based on proximity and dominion over an area where drugs are found.
South Dakota's 'internal possession' statute allows charging based on metabolites in urine alone — unique to SD.
Lab testing of substances is generally uncontested in routine cases.
Schedule I/II covers virtually all street drugs (meth, cocaine, heroin, fentanyl).
defense_opportunities: Challenge constructive possession — mere proximity is insufficient; dominion and control must be proven.
Fourth Amendment suppression for unlawful searches is the most powerful defense.
Challenge the internal possession statute under privacy and equal protection grounds (constitutional challenges have had mixed success).
Contest the lab analysis — substance identification, weight, and chain of custody.
common_defenses: Substance was not actually a controlled substance (lab error).
Constructive possession insufficient (drugs belonged to another).

prosecution_strengths: Internal possession via blood/urine testing is enforceable for marijuana.
Field testing kits provide presumptive identification at scene.
Visible smoke or odor remains valid probable cause in most contexts.
Felony enhancement at 2 oz makes even modest amounts felonies.
defense_opportunities: Medical marijuana cardholders under IM 26 have an affirmative defense for compliant possession.
Hemp and CBD products can produce false positives with field tests — demand lab confirmation.
Odor-based searches face increasing scrutiny in jurisdictions with legal medical marijuana.
Challenge weight calculations, especially when drying or stem inclusion affects classification.
Negotiate to paraphernalia or attempted possession to avoid felony exposure.
common_defenses: Valid medical marijuana card and compliant amount.
Substance was lawful hemp or CBD.
Insufficient quantity for the alleged classification.

prosecution_strengths: Cocaine is unmistakable in lab testing with high reliability.
Internal possession statute applies to cocaine metabolites.
Possession with intent to distribute can be inferred from packaging, scales, or cash.
Schedule II classification removes any defense based on medical use.
defense_opportunities: Suppression of evidence based on illegal search is the strongest defense.
Constructive possession challenges in vehicle/shared residence cases.
Demand independent lab testing of the substance.
Negotiate to attempted possession to reduce felony class.

prosecution_strengths: Methamphetamine is a Schedule II controlled substance — Class 5 Felony for any amount.
Internal possession by metabolites in urine is also a felony in SD.
Meth indicia (pipes, baggies, scales) are commonly found and admissible.
Confidential informants often provide controlled buy evidence.
Meth possession often paired with manufacturing or trafficking charges.
defense_opportunities: Internal possession charges are vulnerable to constitutional privacy challenges and chain of custody attacks on urine samples.
Suppress searches that lacked clear probable cause (odor of meth is harder to establish than alcohol).
Challenge substance identification — over-the-counter decongestants can produce false positives in field tests.
Constructive possession defenses in shared environments.

prosecution_strengths: Threshold quantities create automatic trafficking charges regardless of intent.
Wiretap evidence, controlled buys, and informant testimony build strong cases.
Conspiracy charges can sweep in peripheral participants.
defense_opportunities: Challenge quantity calculations — packaging weight versus pure substance weight.
Attack informant credibility and prior cooperation deals.
Suppress wiretap evidence on minimization and necessity grounds.
Entrapment when informants instigated otherwise non-existent transactions.
Conspiracy requires actual agreement — mere presence or association is insufficient.
common_defenses: Lack of knowing participation in trafficking.

prosecution_strengths: Quantity-based escalation: 1/2 lb of marijuana triggers Class 3 Felony.
Hand-to-hand controlled buys provide compelling evidence.
Cell phone records of drug-related communications are routinely admitted.
defense_opportunities: Distinguish distribution from possession — was there an actual transfer?
Personal use defense when quantity is borderline.
Challenge informant testimony with prior inconsistent statements.
Suppress searches and seizures that produced the underlying drugs.
Negotiate to simple possession when transfer evidence is weak.
common_defenses: Lack of knowledge that the substance was controlled.

prosecution_strengths: Pseudoephedrine purchase tracking under NPLEx provides direct evidence of meth manufacturing.
Lab equipment, precursors, and chemicals create strong circumstantial cases.
Photographs of grow operations are powerful jury evidence.
Marijuana cultivation of any plant count is a felony under SD law.
defense_opportunities: Challenge the existence of an actual manufacturing operation versus possession of items with legal uses.
Pseudoephedrine purchases must connect to manufacturing activity, not personal cold/allergy use.
Suppress searches based on inadequate warrants for residential grow operations.
Medical marijuana defense for compliant cultivation under IM 26.
Challenge plant counts and weight calculations.
common_defenses: Items had lawful purposes (no manufacturing intent).
Lack of knowledge of activities by others on property.
Insufficient evidence linking defendant to operation.

prosecution_strengths: Class 2 Misdemeanor with lower burden of proof.
Visible residue on items often supports charges without separate possession.
Frequently charged alongside possession to maintain leverage.
Even legal items become paraphernalia based on intent or use.
defense_opportunities: Challenge intent — pipes and scales have lawful uses (tobacco, cooking).
Negotiate dismissal in exchange for plea on more serious charge.
Constitutional vagueness challenges to broad paraphernalia definitions.
Suppression of underlying search.
Lack of knowledge of paraphernalia presence.
common_defenses: Item had lawful use and purpose.

prosecution_strengths: Class 4 Felony for first offense — significantly more serious than simple possession.
Cell phone evidence of drug-related communications routinely admitted.
Cash without legitimate source is treated as drug proceeds.
Statements to officers about distribution are powerful admissions.
defense_opportunities: Personal use defense — argue quantity reflects heavy personal use, not distribution.
Cash defense — establish lawful source of money found with drugs.
Challenge inferences from packaging when defendant purchased pre-packaged.
Suppress search that produced the indicia of distribution.
Negotiate down to simple possession.
common_defenses: Mistaken identification of substance or quantity.

prosecution_strengths: Death penalty eligibility for Class A Felony creates enormous plea leverage.
DNA, ballistic, and forensic evidence carry enormous weight.
South Dakota allows capital aggravating factors that broaden death-eligible cases.
defense_opportunities: Challenge premeditation — heat of passion or impulse defenses can reduce to second-degree.
Mental state defenses (insanity, diminished capacity, intoxication) may negate premeditation.
Challenge identification through eyewitness reliability research.
Forensic challenges to DNA contamination, ballistic match certainty.

prosecution_strengths: Class B Felony with mandatory life without parole.
Often used as a compromise charge during plea negotiations.
Implied malice from reckless conduct can support the charge.
Forensic evidence carries weight regardless of premeditation.
defense_opportunities: Negotiate down to manslaughter by establishing heat of passion or imperfect self-defense.
Challenge implied malice — mere recklessness may not suffice.
Self-defense defenses can fully exonerate.
Challenge causation, especially in attenuated circumstances.
Mental state defenses including voluntary intoxication negating specific intent.
common_defenses: Lack of malice or knowing conduct.

prosecution_strengths: Class C Felony with significant exposure (up to life).
Often used as a fallback when murder charges face self-defense issues.
Provocation can be physical or verbal in some circumstances.
Plea negotiations frequently land here from initial murder charges.
defense_opportunities: Self-defense remains a complete defense and can result in acquittal.
Challenge whether the provocation was 'adequate' — words alone are generally insufficient.
Cooling-off period analysis — too much time between provocation and act negates the charge.
Imperfect self-defense in some scenarios.
Causation challenges in attenuated cases.

prosecution_strengths: Class 4 Felony with up to 10 years exposure.
Lower mens rea standard makes conviction easier than higher homicide charges.
Frequently charged in DUI fatalities, child endangerment deaths, and weapon accidents.
Misdemeanor manslaughter rule allows charges where death results from any unlawful act.
defense_opportunities: Argue conduct was at most ordinary negligence, not criminal.
Challenge causation — was the negligent act the proximate cause?
Intervening cause defenses are common.
Accident defense when no underlying unlawful act occurred.
Constitutional challenges to misdemeanor manslaughter rule.
common_defenses: Conduct did not rise to criminal negligence.
Pure accident with no underlying misconduct.

prosecution_strengths: Class 3 Felony with up to 15 years exposure.
Photographic evidence of injuries is powerful jury evidence.
911 calls are admissible as excited utterances.
Domestic violence enhancement applies in many household contexts.
defense_opportunities: South Dakota recognizes 'stand your ground' principles in some contexts.
Challenge 'serious bodily injury' classification — temporary injuries may not qualify.
Mutual combat defense in bar fights and similar scenarios.
Challenge identification when assailant is not clearly identified.
common_defenses: Lack of intent to cause serious injury.

prosecution_strengths: Class 1 Misdemeanor with quick disposition possible.
Third or subsequent offense within 5 years escalates to Class 6 Felony.
Verbal threats accompanied by gestures can suffice.
Officer testimony about visible injuries is generally credible.
defense_opportunities: Self-defense applies even to simple assault charges.
Mutual combat negates one-sided assault claims.
Challenge whether the alleged conduct put the victim in actual fear.
Negotiate to disorderly conduct as a lesser offense.
Lack of intent — accidental contact is not assault.

prosecution_strengths: Any unwanted physical contact can suffice.
Visible injuries are not required for conviction.
Often charged in conjunction with assault for charging leverage.
defense_opportunities: Self-defense and defense of others.
Accidental contact defense.
Mutual combat in physical altercations.
Lack of intent to make contact.
Consent (in sporting events, certain physical interactions).

prosecution_strengths: Class 2 Felony with up to 25 years exposure.
Force element is broadly construed — any physical contact during the taking suffices.
Surveillance video and eyewitness identification provide strong evidence.
Implied threats with no weapon present can still qualify.
defense_opportunities: Challenge identification through eyewitness reliability research.
Distinguish robbery from theft — was force or fear actually used?
Claim of right defense when defendant believed property was lawfully theirs.
Mistaken identity is the most common successful defense.
Challenge the force element — was it incidental to the taking or used to overcome resistance?

prosecution_strengths: Class 2 Felony with up to 25 years and strong jury sympathy.
Visible firearms in surveillance video are highly persuasive.
Co-defendant testimony often available through plea cooperation.
defense_opportunities: Challenge weapon identification — was it actually a firearm or a replica/toy?
Suppress eyewitness identifications through reliability challenges.
Co-defendant testimony is impeachable through cooperation deals.
Mere presence at the scene is not robbery.
Withdrawal from criminal enterprise before commission.

prosecution_strengths: Class C Felony with up to life imprisonment.
Class 1 Felony if victim suffers serious injury (mandatory life).
Even brief detentions can support kidnapping charges.
Frequently charged with sexual assault or robbery to enhance exposure.
defense_opportunities: Challenge whether the movement or confinement was substantial — incidental movements during another crime may not support separate kidnapping charges.
Consent of the alleged victim is a defense.
Parental defense for noncustodial parents in family disputes (some limits apply).
Lack of specific intent to hold for required purposes.
Constitutional challenges to overlapping kidnapping/robbery convictions.
common_defenses: Movement was merely incidental to another offense.

prosecution_strengths: Class 2 Felony with up to 25 years exposure.
Fire investigators provide expert testimony on origin and cause.
Insurance fraud investigations often uncover arson motives.
Accelerant residue analysis is generally admissible.
defense_opportunities: Challenge fire investigator's origin and cause analysis — modern arson science has discredited many traditional 'indicators.'
Demand independent fire science expert review.
Accidental fire defenses are increasingly successful with modern science.
Insurance company motives for finding arson can bias investigations.
Alibi defenses when defendant was demonstrably elsewhere.

prosecution_strengths: Specific intent to kill plus a substantial step is sufficient.
Victim survival evidence is powerful.
Statements of intent are highly damaging.
Often charged alongside aggravated assault for charging leverage.
defense_opportunities: Challenge specific intent to kill — assault or recklessness is not attempted murder.
Self-defense applies fully to attempted murder charges.
Challenge whether the action was a 'substantial step' or mere preparation.
Negotiate to aggravated assault when intent is borderline.
common_defenses: Lack of specific intent to kill.

prosecution_strengths: 'Dangerous weapon' is broadly defined to include any object capable of inflicting serious harm.
Vehicles, broken bottles, and household objects can qualify.
Brandishing alone may suffice if intended to intimidate.
Photographic evidence of weapons enhances jury impact.
defense_opportunities: Self-defense applies fully and is broadly construed in SD.
Challenge whether the object qualified as a 'dangerous weapon' under the circumstances.
Mere possession of a weapon during a verbal altercation is not assault.
Mistaken identity defenses.
Negotiate to simple assault when weapon involvement is unclear.
common_defenses: Object was not a dangerous weapon under circumstances.

prosecution_strengths: Felony threshold begins at $1,000 — relatively low compared to other states.
Aggregation rule allows multiple thefts within a single course of conduct to be combined for charging.
Constructive possession theories support theft from joint accounts and shared property.
Restitution is mandatory and creates additional financial pressure.
defense_opportunities: Challenge value calculations — fair market value at time of theft, not replacement cost.
Claim of right defense when defendant believed property was lawfully owed.
Civil dispute defense — many alleged thefts are actually contract disputes.
Challenge the aggregation theory when incidents are unrelated.
Negotiate to a misdemeanor when value is borderline.
common_defenses: Lack of intent to permanently deprive.

prosecution_strengths: Bank records and financial documents create strong paper trails.
Aggregation of multiple smaller thefts can reach grand theft thresholds.
Identity theft and embezzlement often charged as grand theft.
Restitution amounts create powerful plea leverage.
defense_opportunities: Challenge value calculations meticulously — small adjustments can reduce felony class.
Claim of right defenses for disputed property.
Forensic accounting can show legitimate transactions misclassified as theft.
Statute of limitations defenses for older transactions.
Negotiate restitution-based dispositions to avoid conviction.
common_defenses: Insufficient value to support felony class.
Lack of intent to permanently deprive.
Authorization to take or use the property.

prosecution_strengths: Surveillance video commonly captures the act.
Store loss prevention testimony is generally credible.
Recovery of stolen merchandise is direct evidence.
Often charged alongside trespassing or other offenses.
defense_opportunities: Diversion programs are commonly available for first-time petty theft offenders.
Challenge intent — defendant may have intended to pay or believed payment was made.
Suspended imposition of sentence preserves clean record.
Challenge the value if it affects classification.
Negotiate dismissal with restitution and community service.
common_defenses: Reasonable belief of right to take the property.

prosecution_strengths: Loss prevention officers in retail settings provide professional witnesses.
Surveillance video makes most cases self-proving.
Aggregation across multiple incidents can reach felony levels.
defense_opportunities: Challenge the concealment-equals-intent presumption.
Forgetfulness or distraction defenses for items in carts or hands.
First-time offender diversion programs.
Challenge value when discounts or sale prices apply.

prosecution_strengths: Class 2 Felony with up to 25 years exposure.
Intent can be inferred from circumstances — tools, time of day, manner of entry.
DNA, fingerprints, and surveillance commonly available.
Confederate cooperation is common in burglary rings.
defense_opportunities: Challenge the intent element — was there actual intent to commit a crime inside, or mere unlawful entry?
Trespass is a lesser included offense available for negotiation.
Permission to enter defense for ambiguous relationships.
Mistaken identity from limited identification evidence.
Withdrawal before completion of intended crime.
common_defenses: Lack of intent to commit a crime inside.
Mistake of fact regarding ownership/right to enter.

prosecution_strengths: Occupancy enhancement applies when residents are home.
Home security systems and Ring/doorbell cameras provide modern evidence.
DNA evidence on touched surfaces is increasingly probative.
Strong jury sympathy for residential victims.
defense_opportunities: Permission to enter from a household member.
Challenge the 'dwelling' classification for outbuildings or unoccupied properties.
Eyewitness identification is often unreliable, especially in nighttime entries.
Mistaken identity defenses.
Lack of intent if defendant was confused or impaired.

prosecution_strengths: VIN tracking and license plate readers identify stolen vehicles quickly.
Insurance reports provide documentation of value and theft.
Joyriding can be charged as theft if intent to deprive can be shown.
Often combined with other charges like fleeing or possession of burglary tools.
defense_opportunities: Joyriding defense — temporary use without intent to permanently deprive (lesser offense).
Permission of the owner defense.
Mistaken identity in cases of recovered abandoned vehicles.
Negotiate to unauthorized use of motor vehicle.
Challenge value calculations for older vehicles.
common_defenses: Lack of intent to permanently deprive.

prosecution_strengths: Constructive knowledge can be inferred from circumstances (price, source, condition).
Possession of recently stolen property creates a presumption of knowledge.
Pawn shop records are easily subpoenaed.
Same classification scale as theft based on value.
defense_opportunities: Challenge the knowledge element — defendant must have known or reasonably should have known.
Innocent purchaser defense for legitimate transactions.
Challenge the value affecting classification.
Challenge identification of property as actually stolen.
Suppression of search that produced the property.
common_defenses: Lack of knowledge that property was stolen.

prosecution_strengths: Felony threshold at $1,000 is relatively low.
Surveillance video and graffiti tag identification provide direct evidence.
Restitution requirements create plea leverage.
Multiple incidents can be aggregated for charging.
defense_opportunities: Challenge damage estimates — actual repair cost, not inflated estimates.
Lack of intent for accidental damage.
Civil dispute defense for boundary disputes and joint property.
Mistaken identity defenses.
Negotiate to a lesser misdemeanor when value is borderline.
common_defenses: Insufficient damage value for felony classification.

prosecution_strengths: No-trespass orders create easy enforcement.
Body camera footage of warnings creates clear records.
Repeat offenses escalate to Class 1 Misdemeanor.
Often used as a base charge to support other allegations.
defense_opportunities: Public access defense for ostensibly public spaces.
Necessity defense for emergencies.
Challenge the specific date and time of alleged trespass.
Negotiate dismissal for first offense.

prosecution_strengths: Same classification scale as vandalism by damage value.
Surveillance and witness evidence easily obtained.
Restitution mandatory.
Often charged in domestic disputes for damage to shared property.
defense_opportunities: Same defenses as vandalism apply.
Joint ownership defense for damage to shared property.
Challenge damage estimates.
Mistake of fact about ownership.
Negotiate to lower offense or restitution-based disposition.

prosecution_strengths: Subsequent offenses escalate to felony quickly.
Excited utterance and 911 call evidence routinely admitted.
Protection order violations can be charged additionally.
defense_opportunities: False allegation defense — common in custody and divorce contexts.
Self-defense applies in domestic settings.
Mutual combat defense for fights between intimate partners.
Recantation by the alleged victim, though prosecutors may proceed without victim cooperation.
Challenge the household member relationship element.

prosecution_strengths: Visible injuries documented with photographs are powerful evidence.
911 calls and excited utterances are admissible.
Federal Lautenberg Amendment firearm prohibition follows conviction.
Mandatory arrest policies mean charges are nearly automatic.
defense_opportunities: Self-defense is the strongest defense.
Mutual combat defense.
Lack of intent (accidental contact).
False allegation in custody disputes.
Negotiate to disorderly conduct to avoid Lautenberg consequences.

prosecution_strengths: Class 4 Felony with significant exposure.
DUI with child passenger triggers automatic enhancement.
Subjective endangerment standard makes prosecution easier.
DCS investigations often run parallel and create additional pressure.
defense_opportunities: Challenge whether the conduct created a 'substantial risk' as opposed to minor risk.
Parental discretion defense for ordinary parenting decisions.
Lack of knowledge defense when child was unexpectedly present.
Cultural or generational parenting practice defenses (limited).
Negotiate to misdemeanor child neglect when borderline.

prosecution_strengths: Mandatory reporters create cascading evidence sources.
Medical examination evidence carries strong weight.
Pediatric forensic specialists are available as experts.
Prior CPS involvement is admissible in some circumstances.
defense_opportunities: Challenge medical findings — many alleged abuse injuries have benign explanations (mongolian spots, hair follicle conditions, accidental injuries).
Reasonable parental discipline defense (limited but available).
Mistaken identity in households with multiple caregivers.
Suggestibility of child witnesses, especially under repeated questioning.
Forensic interviewer protocol challenges.

prosecution_strengths: No proof of harm required — mere contact violates the order.
Phone records, text messages, and social media create easy documentation.
Third-party contact through intermediaries also violates the order.
Subsequent violations within 10 years escalate to Class 6 Felony.
defense_opportunities: Challenge whether defendant had actual notice of the order.
Inadvertent contact defense (chance encounter in public).
Necessity defense in emergencies.
Challenge the validity of the underlying order.
Protected party initiated contact (not always a defense but mitigating).
common_defenses: Lack of notice of the order.

prosecution_strengths: Pattern of conduct can be established through multiple incidents.
Subsequent offenses within 10 years escalate to Class 6 Felony.
Electronic communications and GPS tracking provide modern evidence.
Victim's subjective fear is admissible.
defense_opportunities: Challenge whether the conduct was actually 'willful and malicious' versus persistent but lawful contact.
Constitutional First Amendment defenses for protected speech.
Challenge reasonableness of victim's fear in light of all circumstances.
Mistaken identity for online or anonymous contact.
Negotiate to harassment charge.

prosecution_strengths: Phone calls, texts, and online messages provide direct evidence.
Lower bar than stalking — single incidents may suffice in some cases.
Class 1 Misdemeanor with quick disposition.
Often paired with stalking or domestic violence charges.
defense_opportunities: Challenge intent — communication for legitimate purposes is not harassment.
First Amendment defenses for political or critical speech.
Recipient was not actually alarmed or annoyed.
Mistaken identity for online contact.
Negotiate dismissal for first offense.

prosecution_strengths: Class 6 Felony minimum with higher classes for financial exploitation.
Adult Protective Services investigations create parallel evidence sources.
Bank records easily prove financial exploitation.
Strong jury sympathy for elderly victims.
defense_opportunities: Challenge the 'elder' classification — must meet statutory definition.
Authorization defense for financial transactions (powers of attorney, joint accounts).
Family member dispute defenses for inheritance and gift disputes.
Capacity of the elderly person to consent.
Mistaken identity in shared care environments.
common_defenses: Capacity and consent of the elder.

prosecution_strengths: Strict liability in many circumstances.
Possession in prohibited locations (schools, government buildings) creates per se violations.
Officer testimony about visible weapons is generally credible.
Often paired with other charges to enhance plea leverage.
defense_opportunities: Challenge the 'possession' element — constructive possession requires dominion and control.
Lawful possession defenses for permits and exemptions.
Challenge the search that revealed the weapon.
Necessity defense in self-defense situations.
Negotiate to lesser violation.

prosecution_strengths: Class 6 Felony with significant prison exposure.
Prior felony conviction is easily proven through court records.
